set1.q: A 76-year-old man has spells of palpitations and near-fainting. A 24-hour monitor shows runs of a fast rhythm that alternate with slow beats and long pauses (tachy-brady syndrome). Which rhythm most often produces the fast runs?
opts: Ventricular tachycardia can be the fast phase in some patients with tachy-brady syndrome, and then the permanent pacemaker needs an implantable defibrillator as well. It is not the most common fast rhythm; atrial fibrillation is. Tell: ventricular tachycardia changes the device, not the most likely answer.

Atrial flutter is a regular sawtooth rhythm commonly seen with atrial scarring or right-sided heart failure, but it is not the named most-common fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome. That is atrial fibrillation. Tell: the classic fast phase is irregularly irregular without P waves.

Sinus tachycardia is a regular response to a physiologic or pathologic process, with a P wave before each QRS. The fast runs of tachy-brady syndrome are most often atrial fibrillation. Tell: in tachy-brady syndrome, think of the fast phase as atrial fibrillation first.

Correct. Runs of a fast rhythm alternating with slow beats and long pauses, with palpitations and near-fainting, are tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sick sinus syndrome. The tachyarrhythmia that alternates with the symptomatic bradycardia or pauses is most commonly atrial fibrillation.

Junctional rhythm i. QT prolongation
set1.q: A 63-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy is told that his episode of palpitations was sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Which description best fits that rhythm?
opts: Chaotic waves with no true QRS complexes

Chaotic waves with no true QRS complexes describe ventricular fibrillation, which has no pulse. Ventricular tachycardia has organized, regular wide complexes. Tell: chaos is fibrillation; regular wide complexes are tachycardia.
Regular, wide QRS complexes of one shape

Correct. Ventricular tachycardia is regular at 100 to 250 with wide QRS complexes over 0.12 seconds and no P waves. Monomorphic means every complex has the same shape, and sustained means it lasted 30 seconds or more or caused hemodynamic collapse sooner.

Ventricular tachycardia is regular, at 100 to 250, so an irregular rhythm near 300 does not fit, and monomorphic means every QRS has the same shape. A wide rhythm whose QRS shape varies is polymorphic. Tell: monomorphic tachycardia is regular and uniform.
Regular, narrow QRS with hidden P waves

A narrow QRS does not fit ventricular tachycardia: a rhythm starting in the ventricles has wide QRS complexes, over 0.12 seconds, at 100 to 250 with no P waves. Tell: a narrow complex means the beat started above the ventricles.

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with pneumonia and severe hypoxia becomes unresponsive. No pulse can be felt, yet the monitor shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 80 with a P wave before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Ventricular fibrillation is chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no organized QRS complexes. This monitor shows regular, narrow complexes with a P wave before each. Tell: organized complexes rule out fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

The tracing looks like normal sinus rhythm, but she has no pulse. An organized rhythm you would expect to produce a pulse, without perfusing beats, is pulseless electrical activity, a cardiac arrest. Tell: the pulse check, not the monitor, decides the diagnosis.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A regular rhythm at 80 with a P wave before every QRS, which you would expect to produce a pulse, with no pulse is pulseless electrical activity, not asystole. Her severe hypoxia from pneumonia fits one of its two leading causes in adults (hypoxia and hypovolemia), and it is unshockable.

Asystole is a flat line with no P waves and no QRS complexes. This monitor shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm with P waves, which without a pulse is pulseless electrical activity. Tell: pulseless electrical activity is not the same as asystole.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 58-year-old man with chest pain develops a wide tachycardia whose QRS shape varies from beat to beat; his QT interval was normal earlier. He is defibrillated and returns to sinus rhythm. Which study is the most urgent next?
opts: Ambulatory monitoring captures intermittent rhythms over time; it does not address an acute ischemic event. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with chest pain and a normal QT points to ischemia, which needs urgent coronary angiography. Tell: the most urgent study after this rhythm is done in the catheterization lab.

A serum digoxin level does not address the likely cause. Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a normal QT is most commonly from acute ischemia, and he had chest pain, so urgent coronary angiography with possible revascularization comes next. Tell: chest pain plus a normal QT points to ischemia.

A stroke-risk score is not part of the workup after polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. With chest pain and a normal QT, acute ischemia is the likely cause, so urgent coronary angiography comes next. Tell: the priority is the coronary arteries.

Correct. A wide tachycardia whose QRS shape varies is polymorphic ventricular tachycardia; with a normal QT, it is most commonly due to acute myocardial ischemia, and he had chest pain. After defibrillation, the most urgent next step is coronary angiography with possible revascularization.

set1.q: A 20-year-old man with a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 220 converts to sinus rhythm with adenosine. An accessory pathway is suspected. Which tracing is most useful for looking for it?
opts: A coronary angiogram images the coronary arteries and cannot show an accessory pathway, which is an electrical finding. That finding, a short PR and delta wave, appears on a tracing in sinus rhythm. Tell: look for pre-excitation on the sinus-rhythm tracing.

Correct. Pre-excitation, a short PR interval and a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave), on a tracing in normal sinus rhythm is consistent with an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) and the potential for atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia. His narrow tachycardia at 220 that converted with adenosine fits the orthodromic form, so the pathway is sought in sinus rhythm.

A tracing during the tachycardia is not where the pathway is sought. Orthodromic reentry, the more common form, uses antegrade conduction through the atrioventricular node and gives a regular, narrow complex rhythm with a retrograde P wave after the QRS. Pre-excitation, a short PR and delta wave, is documented on tracings in sinus rhythm. Tell: look for the pathway on the sinus-rhythm tracing.

A serum electrolyte panel does not reveal an accessory pathway; electrolyte abnormalities appear instead among causes of sick sinus syndrome. The pathway is found by pre-excitation, a short PR with a delta wave, on a tracing in sinus rhythm. Tell: an accessory pathway is an electrical finding on the tracing, not a laboratory one.

set1.q: A 55-year-old man has a preoperative electrocardiogram and no symptoms. The rhythm is sinus at 72, the QRS lasts 0.16 seconds, V1 to V3 show an rsR' pattern (a second upward deflection, bunny ears), and there is a slurred S wave in I and aVL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A QRS over 0.12 seconds (here 0.16) with an rsR' pattern (bunny ears) in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL is right bundle branch block. It is usually asymptomatic, its treatment depends on any underlying condition, and a new block is not always pathological.

Left bundle branch block widens the QRS with a dominant S wave (rS) in V1 and monophasic R waves in the lateral leads. An rsR' in V1 to V3 with a slurred S in I and aVL is right bundle branch block. Tell: bunny ears in V1 mean right; a deep S in V1 means left.

Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome does not produce rsR' in V1 to V3 with a slurred S in I and aVL. Those findings, with a QRS of 0.16 seconds, are the criteria for right bundle branch block. Tell: bunny ears in the right precordial leads mean right bundle branch block.

Ventricular tachycardia is a regular wide rhythm at 100 to 250 with no P waves. He is in sinus rhythm at 72, so the wide QRS is a conduction delay, here right bundle branch block. Tell: a wide QRS at a normal sinus rate is a bundle branch block.

set1.q: A 24-year-old man collapses during a basketball game and wakes within a minute. In the ambulance his rhythm is irregular, with wide QRS complexes of varying width at rates approaching 300. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial flutter with 2:1 block is a regular rhythm with narrow QRS complexes and two sawtooth flutter waves for every QRS. This rhythm is irregular with wide complexes. Tell: regular and narrow with sawtooth waves is flutter; irregular and wide is pre-excited atrial fibrillation.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular but narrow, with at least three P-wave shapes, and occurs in acutely ill patients with severe lung disease or heart failure. This young athlete has wide complexes at rates near 300. Tell: irregular and narrow with changing P waves is multifocal; irregular and wide near 300 is pre-excited fibrillation.

Correct. An irregular rhythm with wide QRS complexes of varying width at rates approaching 300 is atrial fibrillation conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White, pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Ventricular tachycardia, the look-alike wide rhythm, is regular at 150 to 200, so the irregularity and the rate near 300 settle it.

Ventricular tachycardia is the other wide-complex tachycardia to consider, but it is regular, with rates between 150 and 200. This rhythm is irregular and approaches 300. Tell: wide and regular at 150 to 200 is ventricular tachycardia; wide and irregular near 300 is atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White.

set1.q: A 69-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has a preoperative 12-lead electrocardiogram, which is shown. The QRS lasts 0.16 seconds. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: This tracing does not show a pre-excitation pattern; its deep, dominant S waves in V1 and broad, upright lateral complexes are a bundle branch block. Tell: a QRS over 0.12 seconds with a deep S in V1 and no lateral Q waves is left bundle branch block.

Correct. A QRS of 0.16 seconds with a deep, dominant S wave in V1 (rS pattern) and broad, upright, monophasic lateral complexes without Q waves in I, V5 and V6 is left bundle branch block. Chronic hypertension, her long-standing condition, is a named cause.

Right bundle branch block gives an rsR' pattern ('bunny ears') in V1 to V3 and a slurred S wave in I and aVL. Here V1 to V3 are deep and downward. Tell: bunny ears in V1 mean right; a deep S in V1 means left.

Ventricular tachycardia is a regular wide rhythm at 100 to 250 with no P waves. This preoperative tracing shows wide complexes at a normal rate with a deep S wave in V1, the pattern of a bundle branch block. Tell: wide at a normal rate means slowed conduction, not tachycardia.
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram with wide complexes, deep downward complexes in V1 to V3 and broad upright complexes in the lateral leads

set1.q: A 58-year-old man reports frequent skipped beats. His electrocardiogram shows many early beats, each with an abnormally shaped P wave and a narrow QRS. Which is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?
opts: No treatment is needed for premature atrial contractions that are infrequent and asymptomatic. His are frequent and noticeable, and frequent beats call for a search for structural heart disease. Tell: frequency is the switch; frequent premature atrial contractions get evaluated.

Correct. Many early beats, each with an abnormally shaped P wave and a narrow QRS, are frequent premature atrial contractions. When they are frequent, the next step is to look for underlying structural heart disease, since in a diseased heart they may precede supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter.

Anticoagulation is part of managing atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, guided by stroke risk. Premature atrial contractions are early beats with their own P wave, and frequent ones call for a structural workup instead. Tell: a P wave before each early beat means these are not fibrillation.

Urgent coronary angiography is not the evaluation listed for premature atrial contractions. Frequent ones call for a look for underlying structural heart disease, with counseling to avoid precipitants and a beta blocker if persistent and symptomatic. Tell: frequent premature atrial beats lead to a structural heart workup.

set1.q: A 74-year-old woman has episodes of lightheadedness. Her office electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 64, but her family has noticed a slow pulse during the spells. Which is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
opts: A permanent pacemaker is placed in sick sinus syndrome once symptomatic bradycardia is confirmed, meaning the symptoms correlate with episodes of slow rate. That link has not yet been shown, since her office tracing is normal at 64. Tell: document the slow rate during symptoms before committing to a device.

Urgent coronary angiography does not answer the question her case raises, which is whether her spells correlate with episodes of bradycardia. Sinus node ischemia is one cause of sick sinus syndrome, but intermittent slow spells are first captured with a 24-hour ambulatory recording. Tell: intermittent symptoms with a normal office tracing need ambulatory monitoring.

Observation is appropriate in sick sinus syndrome only if symptoms turn out not to correlate with bradycardia. Her family has noticed a slow pulse during her spells, so that link has to be tested by monitoring before she is reassured. Tell: reassurance comes after monitoring, not instead of it.

Correct. An older woman with lightheaded spells, a normal office tracing and a slow pulse during the spells suggests sick sinus syndrome, and the key step is to confirm whether symptoms correlate with episodes of bradycardia. A 24-hour ambulatory recording does that; with correlation a permanent pacemaker follows, without it observation is appropriate.

set1.q: A 28-year-old woman has had a pounding heartbeat for 30 minutes that began suddenly. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 118/76. The monitor reads a regular rate of 170, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Adenosine is the right drug for stable supraventricular tachycardia, but it comes second, after a vagal maneuver; it may convert the rhythm or slow it enough to show P waves. She is stable, so the drug-free step comes first. Tell: in a stable patient, try the vagal maneuver before any drug.

Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia. She is alert with a blood pressure of 118/76 after 30 minutes, so she is stable. Tell: stable means vagal maneuver, then adenosine; unstable means a timed shock.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. Her strip is regular and narrow without pre-excitation. Tell: a regular narrow tachycardia in a stable patient starts with a vagal maneuver.

Correct. A sudden, regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves is supraventricular tachycardia, here typical slow-fast nodal reentry, and she is alert with a blood pressure of 118/76. In a stable patient a vagal maneuver is first line, followed by adenosine if it fails.
set1.alt: Lead II rhythm strip of a regular, rapid narrow-complex rhythm with no P wave visible before the complexes

set1.q: A 70-year-old woman with hypertension has had palpitations for a week. She is alert, with a blood pressure of 132/80, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the first goal of treatment?
opts: Correct. The strip shows narrow complexes at irregularly irregular intervals with no P waves, which is atrial fibrillation, and with a blood pressure of 132/80 and a clear mind she is hemodynamically stable. Stable atrial fibrillation is managed with rate control, with anticoagulation decided by her stroke-risk score, to which her hypertension and age contribute.

Immediate synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial fibrillation. She is alert with a blood pressure of 132/80, so she is stable, and an elective cardioversion would need 21 days of anticoagulation first. Tell: a shock now needs instability, such as hypotension or pulmonary edema.

Adenosine is a step for stable, regular supraventricular tachycardia, after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Her rhythm is irregularly irregular with no P waves, already recognizable as atrial fibrillation. Tell: an irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves needs rate control, not a diagnostic drug.

Mapping and ablation is one of the later options in managing atrial fibrillation, not the first goal of treatment. A stable patient like her starts with rate control, and anticoagulation is planned for all. Tell: stable atrial fibrillation begins with rate control; procedures come later.
set1.alt: Rhythm strip of narrow complexes at visibly unequal intervals over a wavy baseline with no clear P waves

set1.q: A 48-year-old woman started a medication known to prolong the QT interval last week. She now has palpitations but is awake and talking, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Adenosine is not among the torsades de pointes treatments: intravenous magnesium for a conscious patient, defibrillation if unstable, and lidocaine as the one antiarrhythmic that can be used. Her twisting polymorphic rhythm on a QT-prolonging drug calls for magnesium.

Correct. A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose complexes twist around the baseline in a patient with a long QT is torsades de pointes; in a conscious patient intravenous magnesium breaks it, then more magnesium as an infusion.
Amiodarone (like procainamide) is avoided in torsades de pointes because it prolongs the QT further; magnesium is the treatment.
Beta blockers are avoided in torsades de pointes: the bradycardia they cause lengthens the R-to-R interval and indirectly the QT.
set1.alt: Rhythm strip of a rapid, wide-complex rhythm whose complexes grow taller, shrink, then grow again, as if turning around the baseline

set1.q: A 40-year-old man has a stable, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 180. It is unclear whether the rhythm comes from a focus in the atria or a reentry circuit that uses the atrioventricular node. Which agent is most useful as a diagnostic tool?
opts: Correct. For a stable, regular narrow tachycardia at 180 of unclear origin, adenosine is an important diagnostic tool because it is usually less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia than the node-dependent reentry rhythms. If the rhythm stops, a circuit through the node is likely; if the atrial rhythm carries on, an atrial focus is.

Amiodarone may be tried for chemical cardioversion of focal atrial tachycardia, a treatment step rather than a test. Its effect does not separate an atrial focus from a circuit through the atrioventricular node. Tell: the diagnostic agent is the one whose success or failure differs between the two rhythms, which is adenosine.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or when adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. It is a treatment for that setting, not a diagnostic test for a regular narrow tachycardia. Tell: in a stable regular narrow rhythm of unclear origin, adenosine is the agent that sorts an atrial focus from nodal reentry.

Magnesium has no stated role in sorting out a regular narrow-complex tachycardia. The agent used diagnostically is adenosine, because it usually terminates reentry that depends on the atrioventricular node but is less effective at terminating focal atrial tachycardia. Tell: a diagnostic agent must behave differently in the two rhythms, and adenosine does.

set1.q: A 35-year-old woman has abrupt-onset palpitations. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 170, with one P wave of the same abnormal shape before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia has a uniform, normal P wave before every QRS and runs at over 100 to 160. Her P waves have an abnormal shape and her rate is 170 with an abrupt onset. Tell: the P-wave shape decides it; normal means sinus, consistently abnormal means an ectopic atrial focus.
ruled out by a stated finding

Nodal reentrant tachycardia is a reentry circuit within the atrioventricular node, and its P waves are hidden. She has a visible abnormal P wave before every QRS. Tell: when you can see an abnormal P wave before each QRS, the rhythm is atrial; hidden P waves point to the node.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 170 with one consistently abnormal P wave before every QRS comes from a single ectopic focus in the atria outside the sinus node: focal atrial tachycardia. It usually runs at 150 to 250, and most people report abrupt-onset palpitations, as she does.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three different P-wave shapes in the same lead, and occurs in acutely ill patients with lung disease or heart failure. Her rhythm is regular with one P-wave shape. Tell: one abnormal shape in a regular rhythm is focal; three or more shapes in an irregular rhythm is multifocal.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman has had stable atrial fibrillation for 2 months. Her rate is now controlled, but she would like her normal rhythm restored. Which must come before an outpatient cardioversion?
opts: Correct. Her atrial fibrillation is stable and rate controlled, and she wants sinus rhythm restored electively. Outpatient cardioversion is done after 21 days of anticoagulation, and anticoagulation is part of the plan for all patients with atrial fibrillation unless bleeding risk is high.

Adenosine is a step in stable supraventricular tachycardia, given after a vagal maneuver to convert a regular narrow rhythm or slow it enough to reveal P waves. Her atrial fibrillation is already diagnosed and controlled, so there is nothing to unmask. Tell: preparing for elective cardioversion of atrial fibrillation means 21 days of anticoagulation.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome with symptomatic slow rates. She has a controlled atrial fibrillation and wants her rhythm restored, which calls for 21 days of anticoagulation before an outpatient cardioversion. Tell: pacemakers answer slow rhythms, not elective conversion of a fast one.

Rate control is the listed management for stable atrial fibrillation without rapid ventricular response, and stopping it is not the prerequisite for cardioversion. What must come first for an outpatient cardioversion is 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: the prerequisite is about clot and stroke risk, not about the rate.

set1.q: A 30-year-old marathon runner has no symptoms. A lead II tracing taken at rest is shown; the rate is 48. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves, often at 110 to 160. These complexes are slow, at 48, and evenly spaced. Tell: both lack visible P waves, but a regular slow rhythm is junctional, while fibrillation is irregularly irregular.

Correct. The lead II tracing shows evenly spaced, narrow QRS complexes at 48 with no P wave before any of them because the P waves are hidden in the QRS: a junctional rhythm, usually 40 to 60. It can be seen in healthy people with increased vagal tone, such as this well-conditioned runner, and needs no treatment when asymptomatic.

Sinus bradycardia, which is also seen in conditioned athletes, keeps a uniform P wave before every QRS with a PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. This tracing shows no P wave before any complex. Tell: same slow rate in the same kind of patient, so look for the P wave; hidden P waves mean junctional.
ruled out by a stated finding

Complete atrioventricular block is one cause of a junctional rhythm, and then a permanent pacemaker is needed, but nothing here suggests block: he is an asymptomatic runner with increased vagal tone. The tracing shows regular narrow complexes at 48 with hidden P waves. Tell: the question asks for the rhythm on the strip, and that is junctional.
set1.alt: Lead II rhythm strip of five narrow complexes at a slow, regular rate, each followed by a T wave, with no P wave visible before any complex

set1.q: A 70-year-old man with prior cardiac surgery has a regular rhythm at 150 with sawtooth atrial waves, two for every narrow QRS. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 128/78. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for hemodynamically unstable atrial flutter. He is alert with a blood pressure of 128/78, so rate control comes first, and an elective outpatient cardioversion would follow 21 days of anticoagulation. Tell: stable flutter gets rate control; unstable flutter gets the shock.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White. His rhythm is atrial flutter with 2:1 block and no pre-excitation. Tell: stable flutter is rate controlled with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, not a fast atrial rhythm. His flutter at 150 needs rate control now, with ablation as the definitive management later. Tell: a pacemaker does not treat a fast rhythm; flutter gets rate control, then ablation.

Correct. A regular rate of 150 with two sawtooth waves for every narrow QRS is atrial flutter with 2:1 block, and prior cardiac surgery is a common setting. He is alert with a blood pressure of 128/78, so stable flutter is treated with a beta blocker or calcium channel blocker for rate control, which is harder to achieve than in atrial fibrillation.

set1.q: A 67-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has palpitations and dyspnea. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 150, with two sawtooth atrial waves before every QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sinus tachycardia has one uniform P wave before every QRS, at over 100 to 160. She has two sawtooth waves for each QRS, so the atria are beating twice as fast as the ventricles. Tell: one normal P wave per QRS is sinus; two sawtooth waves per QRS is flutter.

Focal atrial tachycardia has one consistent abnormal P wave per QRS from a single focus, usually at 150 to 250. Two sawtooth waves for every QRS mean the atrial rate is double the ventricular rate, which is atrial flutter with 2:1 block. Tell: one atrial wave per QRS is focal; two in a sawtooth line is flutter.

Correct. Two sawtooth atrial waves before every narrow QRS mean the atria fire near 300 while the node passes every other impulse: atrial flutter with 2:1 block, the most common pattern, giving a regular rate of 150. Flutter is commonly seen with pulmonary vascular disease, such as her pulmonary hypertension.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no organized atrial activity. Her rhythm is regular with repeating sawtooth waves. Tell: organized sawtooth waves with a regular ventricular rate mean flutter; a chaotic baseline with an irregular rate means fibrillation.

set1.q: A 17-year-old soccer player had an episode of racing heartbeat that stopped on its own. His resting tracing, taken in sinus rhythm, is shown. Which description best fits this tracing?
opts: Short PR with a slurred QRS upstroke

Correct. On his resting tracing in sinus rhythm, the P wave runs almost straight into a QRS whose upstroke is slurred: a short PR interval with a delta wave. That is pre-excitation, consistent with an accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) and Wolff-Parkinson-White, which fits his self-terminating episode of racing heartbeat.
Long PR with every P wave conducted

A long PR interval is not this tracing; the P wave runs almost straight into the QRS, so the PR is short, under 0.12 seconds. Combined with the slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave), that short PR marks pre-excitation through an accessory pathway. Tell: in Wolff-Parkinson-White the PR is short, never long.
Progressively longer PR, then a dropped beat

A PR interval that lengthens until a beat drops is not what this tracing shows; every P wave here is followed by a QRS. The striking features are a short PR and a slurred start to each QRS (delta wave), which is pre-excitation. Tell: look at the start of the QRS; a slurred upstroke means an accessory pathway.
Irregular rhythm with no P waves

An irregular rhythm with no P waves describes atrial fibrillation. This tracing was taken in sinus rhythm, with a P wave before every QRS. Tell: in sinus rhythm the clues to an accessory pathway are a short PR and a delta wave, not irregularity.
ruled out by a stated finding

set1.q: A 29-year-old woman has had a resting heart rate of 110 to 120 for months, with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS. Thyroid tests, blood count, oxygen saturation and a drug screen are normal, and she takes no medications or stimulants. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. A resting rate of 110 to 120 for months with a normal P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus tachycardia, and normal thyroid tests, blood count, oxygen saturation and drug screen with no medications or stimulants exclude the secondary causes. A sinus tachycardia unexplained after that search is inappropriate sinus tachycardia, a diagnosis of exclusion.

Appropriate sinus tachycardia is a response to physiologic stress, an underlying pathologic condition or medication effects, and is managed by treating that cause. Her thyroid tests, blood count, oxygen saturation and drug screen are normal and she takes nothing, so no cause remains. Tell: once every secondary cause is excluded, the sinus tachycardia is inappropriate.
ruled out by a stated finding

Focal atrial tachycardia comes from a single ectopic focus outside the sinus node, with a consistently abnormal P wave, usually at 150 to 250, and patients report abrupt-onset palpitations. Her P waves are normal and her rate has sat at 110 to 120 for months. Tell: a normal P-wave shape points sinus; an abnormal one points to an ectopic focus.

Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, outnumbering the QRS complexes. She has one normal P wave before each QRS at 110 to 120. Tell: one normal P wave per QRS keeps the rhythm sinus; extra sawtooth waves mean flutter.

set1.q: An 84-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has fatigue and dizziness. Her electrocardiogram shows P waves and wide QRS complexes at two separate rates with no relationship, the ventricular rate 36. She has had no tick bites, infections or recent procedures. Which cause of this rhythm is most likely?
opts: Bacterial endocarditis with an associated abscess is a listed cause of complete block, but she has had no infection. Degenerative conduction disease of old age and hypertension is the most common cause. Tell: without an infection, an abscess cannot explain the block.
ruled out by a stated finding

Lyme carditis is a listed cause of complete block, but she has had no tick bites. In an 84-year-old with long-standing hypertension, the most common cause is degenerative conduction disease. Tell: the stem rules out the infectious causes on purpose.
ruled out by a stated finding

Increased vagal tone is a cause of first-degree and Mobitz type I block, not complete block, and it does not fit an 84-year-old. Degenerative conduction disease, driven by age and hypertension, is the most common cause. Tell: vagal tone belongs to the milder blocks.

Correct. P waves and wide QRS complexes at two unrelated rates, with a ventricular rate of 36, are complete block. Its most common cause is acquired disease of the conduction system, especially degenerative change from old age, chronic hypertension and diabetes, and she is 84 with long-standing hypertension and no infection or procedure.

set1.q: A 19-year-old woman has had three episodes of a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 230 that converted with adenosine. Her tracing in sinus rhythm shows a short PR interval and a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave). Which is the first-line long-term treatment?
opts: A pill-in-the-pocket beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is an option for nodal reentrant tachycardia, a circuit within the node. Her short PR and delta wave reveal an accessory pathway, and Wolff-Parkinson-White is managed long term by ablating it. Tell: pill in pocket goes with nodal reentry; ablation goes with a delta wave.

Correct. Recurrent regular narrow tachycardia at 230 that converts with adenosine, plus a short PR and slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave) in sinus rhythm, is reentry through an accessory pathway: Wolff-Parkinson-White. For chronic management, catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line treatment.

Oral beta blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are the initial chronic therapy for focal atrial tachycardia. In Wolff-Parkinson-White, catheter ablation of the accessory pathway is the first-line long-term treatment. Tell: a delta wave in sinus rhythm means the long-term answer is ablation, not daily drugs.

A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, as in sick sinus syndrome. Her problem is a fast reentry circuit through an accessory pathway, not a slow rate. Tell: a delta wave points to a pathway to remove, and catheter ablation removes it.

set1.q: A 26-year-old woman with asthma used her inhaler repeatedly during an attack and then felt a sudden, rapid pounding in her chest. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves. Which factor most likely triggered this rhythm?
opts: Correct. A sudden, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves in a young woman is nodal reentrant tachycardia, which may start spontaneously or with exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists or sympathomimetics. Repeated puffs of her rescue inhaler delivered a beta-agonist just before the onset.

Increased vagal tone causes slow rhythms, such as a junctional rhythm in well-conditioned athletes, and vagal maneuvers are what terminate nodal reentry. Raising vagal tone would stop this tachycardia, not start it. Tell: vagal stimulation is the treatment for nodal reentry, not the trigger.

Hypothyroidism is listed among causes of sinus bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome, conditions that slow the heart. It is not among the triggers of nodal reentry, and her rhythm is fast and sudden. Tell: thyroid underactivity belongs on the slow list; her trigger is the inhaler she just used.

Low potassium is not among the listed triggers of nodal reentrant tachycardia, which are exertion, caffeine, alcohol, beta-agonists and sympathomimetics. Electrolyte abnormalities instead appear among the causes of sick sinus syndrome. Tell: the clue in the stem is the repeated inhaler use just before the onset.

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman on several medications has recurrent palpitations and near-fainting. Monitoring shows runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose QRS complexes twist around the baseline (torsades de pointes), and her QT interval is prolonged. Which laboratory abnormality would most likely contribute?
opts: Low hemoglobin is not a named cause of acquired long QT. The named causes are drugs that prolong the QT, hypokalemia and hypocalcemia, and she takes several medications. Tell: for torsades, check potassium and calcium and review the drug list.

Correct. Most torsades de pointes comes from acquired long QT syndrome, whose named causes include QT-prolonging drugs, hypokalemia and hypocalcemia. With several medications and a prolonged QT, low potassium is the laboratory abnormality most likely to contribute, and it should be corrected.

High potassium is not a named cause of acquired long QT; potassium matters here when it is low. The electrolyte causes listed are hypokalemia and hypocalcemia. Tell: in acquired long QT, the electrolytes are low.

High calcium is a named trigger of premature ventricular contractions, but acquired long QT goes with low calcium, along with low potassium. Tell: calcium is high for premature beats and low for a long QT.

set1.q: A 38-year-old man who drinks several energy drinks a day is told his skipped beats are premature ventricular contractions. Which description best fits these beats?
opts: Early and narrow, with an inverted P wave

An early, narrow beat with an inverted P wave is a premature junctional contraction, which begins in the atrioventricular junction. A ventricular beat is wide and bizarre with no P wave. Tell: a narrow beat started above the ventricles.
Wide, with a slurred upstroke and short PR

A wide beat with a slurred upstroke and short PR is not the description of a premature ventricular contraction. That beat is early, wide and bizarre with no P wave at all, so it has no PR interval. Tell: a beat with no P wave cannot have a short PR.
Early, wide and bizarre, with no P wave

Correct. A premature ventricular contraction begins in the ventricles, so the early beat has a wide (over 0.12 seconds), bizarre QRS and no P wave. His several energy drinks a day supply caffeine and stimulants, named triggers, and these beats are often felt as skipped beats or palpitations in the neck.
Early and narrow, with an abnormal P wave

An early beat with an abnormally shaped P wave is a premature atrial contraction, which begins in the atria. A premature ventricular contraction is wide and bizarre with no P wave. Tell: an abnormal P wave in front points to the atria.

set1.q: A 62-year-old man collapses in a hospital hallway. He is unresponsive with no pulse, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation is started. His monitor strip is shown. Which is the most important next step?
opts: Intravenous amiodarone is added when ventricular fibrillation persists after shocks and epinephrine. The first priority is defibrillation as soon as possible. Tell: shock first; antiarrhythmics come later.

Transcutaneous pacing is the emergent treatment for unstable bradycardia from high-grade block. This pulseless, chaotic rhythm is ventricular fibrillation and needs defibrillation. Tell: a pulseless, chaotic strip is shocked, not paced.

Correct. Chaotic, uncoordinated activity with no organized QRS complexes and no pulse is ventricular fibrillation. It is treated as cardiac arrest: defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion) as soon as possible, then 2 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation, with epinephrine every 3 to 5 minutes and amiodarone if it persists.

Synchronized cardioversion times the shock to a QRS complex, so it is for a tachycardia with a pulse. Ventricular fibrillation has no QRS to time to and no pulse, so it needs defibrillation. Tell: no QRS and no pulse mean an unsynchronized shock.

set1.q: A 76-year-old woman is brought in after fainting twice today. She is pale, with a blood pressure of 84/50, and her lead II rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate emergent treatment?
opts: Adenosine is not among the treatments for heart block, and it would not raise a slow rate. This slow rhythm with dropped QRS complexes is Mobitz type II, and an unstable patient needs transcutaneous pacing. Tell: a slow, blocked rhythm with hypotension needs pacing.
Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia with a pulse. This is a slow rhythm with dropped QRS complexes from Mobitz type II, which needs pacing. Tell: pace the slow, shock the fast.

Correct. P waves at a steady rate with a constant PR, then a P wave with no QRS, is Mobitz type II block. Fainting twice today with a blood pressure of 84/50 makes her unstable, so she needs emergent treatment: atropine, epinephrine or transcutaneous pacing, which bridges her to a permanent pacemaker.

A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for Mobitz type II, but with two faints today and a blood pressure of 84/50, she first needs emergent transcutaneous pacing to bridge her there. Tell: 'emergent' points to the temporary measure, 'definitive' to the permanent one.

set1.q: A 47-year-old woman 5 days after hip surgery has sudden dyspnea, chest pain and a heart rate of 118. Her new electrocardiogram shows a QRS of 0.14 seconds with an rsR' pattern (a second upward deflection) in V1 to V3. Which underlying problem best explains the new conduction finding?
opts: Lyme carditis is a named cause of atrioventricular blocks rather than right bundle branch block, and nothing here suggests a tick exposure. A sudden new right bundle branch block after surgery fits a pulmonary embolism. Tell: match the cause to the acute postoperative story.

An accessory pathway is not among the listed causes of right bundle branch block. Her wide QRS with an rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 (the bunny ears of right bundle branch block) appearing suddenly after surgery fits a pulmonary embolism. Tell: rsR' in V1 means right, and a sudden postoperative onset points to the lungs.

Correct. A QRS of 0.14 seconds with an rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 is right bundle branch block. A sudden increase in right ventricular pressure from a pulmonary embolism is a named cause, and sudden dyspnea, chest pain and a heart rate of 118 five days after hip surgery fit that picture.

Aortic stenosis is a named cause of left bundle branch block rather than right. Her rsR' pattern in V1 to V3 is right bundle branch block, and its sudden onset after surgery fits pulmonary embolism. Tell: rsR' in V1 means right, which points to the right ventricle.

set1.q: A 45-year-old woman who drinks four cups of coffee a day feels occasional skipped beats. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm at 78, interrupted by an early beat with an abnormally shaped P wave followed by a narrow QRS. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A premature junctional contraction is early and narrow, but its P wave is inverted in II, III and aVF, buried in the QRS or after the QRS. This beat has an abnormally shaped P wave before the QRS, the atrial pattern. Tell: inverted, hidden or trailing P waves mean junctional; an early, oddly shaped P wave in front means atrial.

A premature ventricular contraction begins in the ventricles and is early, wide and bizarre with no P wave. This early beat is narrow and has its own P wave in front. Tell: a P wave before a narrow early beat places it above the ventricles.
ruled out by a stated finding

A Mobitz type I block is a conduction block, which produces a missing beat rather than an extra early one. Her tracing shows an early beat with its own abnormal P wave and a narrow QRS, which is a premature atrial contraction. Tell: an early extra beat is ectopic; a block drops a beat.

Correct. An early beat with its own abnormally shaped P wave and a narrow QRS, interrupting sinus rhythm at 78, is a premature atrial contraction beginning in the atria. These beats can occur in normal hearts with excess caffeine, stress or alcohol, fitting her four cups of coffee a day.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man recovering from cardiac surgery is told his slow rhythm is a junctional rhythm. Which description best fits his tracing?
opts: Irregular and narrow, with no visible P waves

An irregular narrow rhythm without P waves describes atrial fibrillation, which is irregularly irregular. A junctional rhythm is regular, and its P waves are inverted, buried in the QRS or after it. Tell: junctional means regular; irregular without P waves means fibrillation.
Regular and narrow, with an upright P before each QRS

An upright P wave before each narrow QRS at a slow rate describes sinus bradycardia, with a PR of 0.12 to 0.20 seconds. Junctional P waves are inverted in II, III and aVF or hidden, with a short or absent PR. Tell: upright P waves mean the sinus node; inverted or hidden ones mean the junction.
Regular and narrow, with inverted or hidden P waves

Correct. A junctional rhythm is regular, usually 40 to 60, with a narrow QRS under 0.12 seconds, and its P waves are inverted in II, III and aVF before the QRS, buried in it or after it. The acute period after cardiac surgery, as in this man, is one of its listed causes.
Regular and wide, with P waves unrelated to the QRS

A junctional rhythm keeps a narrow QRS under 0.12 seconds, and its P waves sit just before, within or just after the QRS rather than appearing at an unrelated rate. A regular, wide rhythm with unrelated P waves does not fit. Tell: narrow complexes with inverted or hidden P waves are junctional.

set2.q: A 77-year-old woman is found unresponsive and pulseless, and chest compressions are started. Her monitor strip is shown, and the same flat tracing appears in every lead. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Defibrillation treats ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. A flat tracing in every lead is asystole, which is unshockable. Tell: a flat line is never shocked; compressions and epinephrine are the treatment.

Synchronized cardioversion needs a QRS complex to time the shock to and is for a patient with a pulse. Asystole has neither and is unshockable. Tell: with no QRS and no pulse, the answer is compressions and epinephrine.

Amiodarone is for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia that persists after shocks. Asystole is treated with high-quality compressions and epinephrine. Tell: antiarrhythmics belong to the shockable side of the arrest algorithm.

Correct. A flat tracing in every lead, with no P waves or QRS complexes, is asystole, which is unshockable. High-quality chest compressions and epinephrine 1 mg (1:10,000) by intravenous or intraosseous push every 3 to 5 minutes are the mainstays, early intubation is considered, and the prognosis is poor.

set2.q: A 58-year-old man who takes a beta blocker has an irregular pulse at a routine visit. He has no symptoms, and his rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: First-degree block is a long but constant PR with every P wave conducted. This strip has a P wave that is not followed by a QRS, after the PR has lengthened. Tell: any dropped beat moves the rhythm beyond first degree.
ruled out by a stated finding

Third-degree block shows no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes. On this strip the conducted beats keep a PR that lengthens in a repeating pattern, so the atria and ventricles are still linked. Tell: a predictable PR pattern rules out complete block.

Correct. The PR grows longer beat by beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, then the cycle restarts, which explains the irregular pulse: second-degree Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block. Beta blockers are a named cause, and since he has no symptoms, the block itself needs no treatment.

Mobitz type II keeps a constant PR before randomly dropped QRS complexes. On this strip the PR lengthens progressively before each drop. Tell: a lengthening PR before the drop is type I; a constant PR is type II.
set2.alt: Rhythm strip with small upright P waves and narrow complexes in groups, with a gap where one P wave stands alone

set2.q: An 80-year-old woman with heart failure and atrial fibrillation has nausea and fatigue. Her electrocardiogram now shows a regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 46 with no visible P waves. Which of her medications best explains this rhythm?
opts: Anticholinergic drugs are a listed cause of sinus tachycardia, a fast rhythm with a P wave before each QRS. Her rhythm is slow at 46 with no visible P waves, a junctional rhythm. Tell: anticholinergics speed the heart; a slow junctional rhythm on a heart-failure regimen points to digoxin.

Correct. A regular, narrow-complex rhythm at 46 with no visible P waves is a junctional rhythm, usually 40 to 60, and digoxin toxicity is one of its listed causes. Her nausea and fatigue while taking medicines for heart failure and atrial fibrillation fit that cause, which is treated with atropine and/or digoxin immune Fab (fragment antigen-binding).

Apixaban is a direct oral anticoagulant, preferred for stroke prevention in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation; it is not a listed cause of junctional rhythm. Of her likely medications, digoxin is the one listed as a cause. Tell: anticoagulants protect against stroke; digoxin toxicity slows the heart into a junctional rhythm.

Beta-agonists and sympathomimetics are listed triggers of fast rhythms such as nodal reentrant tachycardia. Her rhythm is slow at 46 with no visible P waves. Tell: a drug that speeds the heart cannot explain a slow junctional rhythm; digoxin toxicity can.

set2.q: A 64-year-old woman with heart failure has had a regular, wide-complex tachycardia at 150 for 40 minutes, every QRS the same shape. She is alert, with no chest pain or shortness of breath and a blood pressure of 126/78. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, a polymorphic tachycardia of a long QT. Her complexes are all one shape, so this is monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, treated with an intravenous antiarrhythmic. Tell: magnesium is for twisting complexes, not identical ones.

Correct. A regular wide tachycardia of one shape for 40 minutes is sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia, often seen with heart failure. She is hemodynamically stable, so it is pharmacologically cardioverted with an intravenous antiarrhythmic; amiodarone suits her, since procainamide is avoided in congestive heart failure.

Defibrillation (unsynchronized cardioversion) is for pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. She is alert with a pulse and a blood pressure of 126/78, so she gets pharmacologic cardioversion. Tell: no pulse means defibrillation; a stable patient with a pulse gets drugs.

Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse, marked by chest pain, altered mental status, shortness of breath or hypotension. She has none of these, so she gets pharmacologic cardioversion. Tell: a stable patient gets a drug first.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man with obesity and sleep apnea notices a fluttering heartbeat. His pulse is irregular at 130. The electrocardiogram shows narrow QRS complexes at irregularly irregular intervals with no P waves and no measurable PR interval. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular too, but it has a P wave before every QRS in at least three different shapes. He has no P waves at all. Tell: in an irregular narrow rhythm, multiple P shapes mean multifocal; absent P waves mean fibrillation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Atrial flutter shows sawtooth waves at an atrial rate of 250 or more, and with a fixed block such as 2:1 it is regular. His tracing has no atrial waves and no pattern to the intervals. Tell: organized sawtooth waves mean flutter; no atrial waves and irregularly irregular intervals mean fibrillation.

Sinus arrhythmia keeps a uniform P wave before every QRS at 60 to 100, with a rate that rises on inspiration and falls on expiration. He has no P waves and a rate of 130. Tell: sinus arrhythmia is irregular with a pattern; atrial fibrillation is irregular with none.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Narrow QRS complexes at irregularly irregular intervals with no P waves and no PR interval are atrial fibrillation, here at 130, within its usual 110 to 160. Obesity, sleep apnea and older age, all present in this man, are among the conditions in which it is commonly seen.

set2.q: A 69-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes has newly found atrial fibrillation, now rate controlled. Her HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score is 1, low risk. Which tool now decides whether she needs anticoagulation?
opts: QRS duration is a feature of the tracing, and atrial fibrillation keeps a narrow QRS under 0.12 seconds; width plays no part in the anticoagulation decision. That decision rests on stroke risk, assessed with the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score. Tell: anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is about clot risk, not the intervals on the tracing.

Correct. Her HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score of 1 is low risk, so anticoagulation is acceptable, and whether she needs it is set by the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score. A score of 0 in men or 1 in women is low risk; her age of 65 to 74 (1), female sex (1), hypertension (1) and diabetes (1) give her 4.

Her HAS-BLED (bleeding-risk) score has already done its job: at 1 it is low risk, so anticoagulation is okay, while a score of 3 and up would mean no anticoagulation. It cannot say whether she needs anticoagulation; stroke risk sets that. Tell: bleeding risk decides whether anticoagulation is safe, stroke risk whether it is needed.

Her heart rate guides rate control, which is already achieved. Whether she needs anticoagulation rests on the CHA2DS2-VASc (stroke-risk) score, where 0 in men or 1 in women is low risk and may not require it. Tell: the rate guides rate control; the stroke-risk score guides anticoagulation.

set2.q: A 68-year-old woman admitted with pneumonia has new, frequent early, wide, bizarre beats without P waves on the monitor. Which is the most important initial evaluation?
opts: Correct. Early, wide, bizarre beats without P waves are premature ventricular contractions, mainly caused by hypoxemia or electrolyte imbalance (low potassium, low magnesium, high calcium). In a patient admitted with pneumonia, checking her oxygen level and electrolytes is the most important initial evaluation.

Urgent coronary angiography follows defibrillation of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, not new premature beats. Her early wide beats during pneumonia call first for checking oxygenation and electrolytes. Tell: premature beats in a sick inpatient point to a correctable trigger.

Ambulatory monitoring captures intermittent rhythms over time, but her early beats are already on the monitor. The evaluation that matters is a search for their named causes: hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance. Tell: the rhythm is already captured; find its cause.

A stroke-risk score has no role in evaluating premature ventricular contractions. Their main causes are hypoxemia and electrolyte imbalance, which are checked first in a patient with pneumonia. Tell: look for the cause of the beats, not a risk score.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man who had cardiac surgery last year reports palpitations and fatigue. His blood pressure is normal, and his rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia has one P wave per QRS in at least three different shapes, usually in acutely ill patients with severe lung disease or heart failure. Here several sawtooth waves fall between each pair of QRS complexes. Tell: changing P shapes, one per beat, is multifocal; a repeating sawtooth outnumbering the QRS complexes is flutter.

Sinus tachycardia has one uniform P wave before each QRS at over 100 to 160. This strip has several atrial waves for every QRS in a sawtooth pattern. Tell: one P wave per QRS is sinus; more atrial waves than QRS complexes is flutter.

Correct. Repeating sawtooth flutter waves outnumber the narrow QRS complexes because the atrioventricular node blocks some of the impulses, which is atrial flutter. It is commonly seen with atrial scarring or damage from surgery, as after his cardiac operation, and causes palpitations and fatigue without usually causing collapse.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no organized atrial activity. This strip shows repeating sawtooth waves between the QRS complexes. Tell: an organized sawtooth baseline is flutter; a chaotic baseline with no P waves is fibrillation.

set2.q: A 52-year-old man has an electrocardiogram before a dental procedure. Among normal sinus beats at 74 is an occasional early, narrow QRS preceded by a P wave that is inverted in II, III and aVF, with a PR interval under 0.12 seconds. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A premature atrial contraction begins in the atria and shows an early, abnormally shaped P wave before a narrow QRS. A P wave inverted in II, III and aVF with a PR under 0.12 seconds is the junctional pattern instead. Tell: inversion in II, III and aVF with a short PR places the early beat in the junction, not the atria.

A premature ventricular contraction begins in the ventricles and is early, wide and bizarre with no P wave. This early beat is narrow and carries an inverted P wave with a short PR. Tell: a narrow early beat with a P wave is supraventricular; a wide, bizarre one without a P wave is ventricular.
ruled out by a stated finding

Wolff-Parkinson-White shows pre-excitation, a short PR interval with a slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave), on tracings in normal sinus rhythm. Here the sinus beats are normal and only the occasional early beat has a short PR, with an inverted P wave. Tell: pre-excitation marks the sinus beats; a junctional premature beat is a one-off.

Correct. An occasional early, narrow QRS whose P wave is inverted in II, III and aVF with a PR under 0.12 seconds comes from the atrioventricular junction: a premature junctional contraction. When the top of the node fires first, the atria beat before the ventricles and the PR is short; most people with these beats have no symptoms.

set2.q: A 72-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted in respiratory distress. His pulse is fast and irregular, and his rhythm strip is shown, with arrows marking P waves. Which description best fits this tracing?
opts: Regular, with sawtooth waves between beats

Regular sawtooth waves outnumbering the QRS complexes describe atrial flutter, at an atrial rate of 250 or more. This strip shows separate P waves of varying shape, one before each QRS, at irregular intervals. Tell: one changing P wave per beat is multifocal; a repeating sawtooth is flutter.
Irregular, with several different P-wave shapes

Correct. The strip shows an irregular, narrow-complex tachycardia with a P wave before each QRS whose shape changes from beat to beat, at least three shapes in the same lead: multifocal atrial tachycardia. It is typical of acutely ill patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, as in his respiratory distress.
Irregularly irregular, with no visible P waves

No P waves with an irregularly irregular rhythm describes atrial fibrillation. On this strip the arrows point to P waves, and their shape changes from beat to beat. Tell: if you can mark a P wave before each QRS, the rhythm is not fibrillation.
Regular, with one abnormal P-wave shape

A regular rhythm with one consistently abnormal P wave describes focal atrial tachycardia, from a single ectopic focus. This rhythm is irregular, with P waves of changing shape. Tell: one shape in a regular rhythm is focal; several shapes in an irregular rhythm is multifocal.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman has a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 210 with no visible P waves. She is confused and pale, with a blood pressure of 70/40. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A vagal maneuver is first line only for stable supraventricular tachycardia. She is confused and pale with a blood pressure of 70/40, so she is hemodynamically unstable. Tell: instability skips the vagal maneuver and adenosine and goes straight to synchronized cardioversion.

Correct. A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 210 with no visible P waves is supraventricular tachycardia, and confusion, pallor and a blood pressure of 70/40 make it hemodynamically unstable. That calls for immediate synchronized cardioversion, a timed shock at decreased voltage; collapse like this is expected once the rate passes 200.

An unsynchronized shock is not the treatment for unstable supraventricular tachycardia; the shock used is synchronized, meaning timed, at decreased voltage. She has a regular narrow rhythm with organized complexes to time the shock to. Tell: an organized narrow-complex rhythm in an unstable patient means synchronized cardioversion.

Adenosine follows a vagal maneuver in stable supraventricular tachycardia and may convert the rhythm or slow it to reveal P waves. She is confused and hypotensive, which calls for an immediate synchronized shock rather than a drug. Tell: drugs are for the stable patient; the unstable one gets cardioversion.

set2.q: A 63-year-old man started a new medication 2 weeks ago and now feels tired. His electrocardiogram shows a regular rate of 48 with an upright P wave before every narrow QRS and a PR interval of 0.18 seconds. Which medication class most likely explains this rhythm?
opts: Beta-agonists are listed triggers of fast rhythms such as nodal reentrant tachycardia, and they do not slow the sinus node. His rhythm is sinus bradycardia at 48. Tell: a drug that slows the sinus rate below 60 belongs to the beta blocker, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or digoxin group.

Correct. A regular rate of 48 with an upright P wave before every narrow QRS and a PR of 0.18 seconds is sinus bradycardia. Beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin are its listed drug causes, and fatigue two weeks after starting a new medication fits a beta blocker.

Anticholinergic drugs are listed causes of sinus tachycardia, which would raise the sinus rate above 100. His sinus rhythm is slow at 48. Tell: anticholinergics speed the sinus node; beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers and digoxin slow it.

Stimulants are listed causes of sinus tachycardia, raising the sinus rate. A slow sinus rhythm at 48 points instead to a beta blocker, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or digoxin. Tell: stimulants and anticholinergics sit on the fast list; beta blockers sit on the slow list.

set2.q: A 34-year-old man was bitten by a tick while hiking a month ago and now feels lightheaded. He takes no medications. His electrocardiogram shows the PR interval growing longer with each beat until a P wave is not followed by a QRS, and then the cycle repeats. Which underlying cause is most likely?
opts: Correct. A PR that grows longer with each beat until a QRS drops, then repeats, is Mobitz type I (Wenckebach) block. Lyme disease (Lyme carditis) is a named cause, and a tick bite a month ago in a 34-year-old who takes no medications points to it; other listed causes are vagal tone, medications, ischemia and ablation.

Degenerative change of the conduction system drives blocks in older patients, especially first-degree, Mobitz type II and complete block. In a 34-year-old with a recent tick bite, Lyme carditis fits best. Tell: young age plus a tick bite points to infection, not wear.
ruled out by a stated finding

Digoxin is a listed medication cause of Mobitz type I, but he takes no medications. The recent tick bite points to Lyme carditis. Tell: the stem rules out drugs on purpose so that the exposure stands out.
ruled out by a stated finding
Increased vagal tone is a listed cause of Mobitz type I, but nothing in his history suggests it. The recent tick bite points to Lyme carditis. Tell: the exposure in the stem is the clue to the cause.

set2.q: A 31-year-old woman has sudden palpitations with visible pounding in her neck (frog sign). She is alert, with a blood pressure of 120/74. Her electrocardiogram shows a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Multifocal atrial tachycardia is irregular, with at least three P-wave shapes in one lead, and arises in acutely ill patients with severe lung disease or heart failure. Her rhythm is regular with no visible P waves, and she is a well young woman. Tell: irregular with changing P waves is multifocal; regular with hidden P waves is nodal reentry.

Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves. Her tachycardia is regular, starts suddenly and comes with neck pulsations, which fits nodal reentry. Tell: both may lack visible P waves, so judge the regularity; regular means reentry, irregularly irregular means fibrillation.

Correct. A sudden, regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 170 with no visible P waves in a young woman, plus visible neck pulsations (frog sign), is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia. It is a reentry circuit within the atrioventricular node, usually at 140 to 180 with hidden P waves, and is far more common in women than men.

Focal atrial tachycardia comes from one ectopic atrial focus and shows a consistent abnormal P wave before every QRS. Her P waves are not visible at all, and neck pulsations (frog sign) are a typical complaint in nodal reentry. Tell: a visible abnormal P wave before each QRS points focal; hidden P waves with neck pulsations point nodal reentry.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction wears a 24-hour monitor. It shows several runs of 5 to 8 consecutive wide, identical beats at 150, each lasting under 10 seconds and stopping on its own. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Sustained ventricular tachycardia lasts 30 seconds or more or causes hemodynamic collapse sooner. His runs stop on their own in under 10 seconds without collapse. Tell: under 30 seconds with no collapse means non-sustained.

Premature atrial contractions are single early beats with an abnormally shaped P wave. His runs are wide, identical and consecutive, which places them in the ventricles. Tell: consecutive wide beats are ventricular tachycardia.

Ventricular fibrillation is uncoordinated activity with no pulse and no perfusion. His runs are organized, identical wide beats at 150 that stop on their own. Tell: identical complexes and self-termination rule out fibrillation.

Correct. Three or more consecutive premature ventricular contractions are ventricular tachycardia, and runs lasting under 30 seconds are non-sustained. His identical QRS shapes make it monomorphic, which is often seen with heart disease such as a prior myocardial infarction.

set2.q: A 57-year-old woman whose QT interval became prolonged after starting a new medication has palpitations, and the monitor shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia whose QRS complexes twist around the baseline (torsades de pointes). She is awake, and intravenous magnesium has been given. If an antiarrhythmic is added, which one can be used?
opts: Correct. Her drug-induced long QT and twisting polymorphic rhythm are torsades de pointes; magnesium is the treatment, and intravenous lidocaine is the one antiarrhythmic that can be used, though evidence for it is limited. Amiodarone and procainamide prolong the QT, and beta blockers prolong it indirectly.

Amiodarone prolongs the QT further, so it is avoided in torsades de pointes. It may be added in polymorphic tachycardia without a long QT, but not here. Tell: with a long QT, the one antiarrhythmic allowed is lidocaine.

Procainamide prolongs the QT, so it is avoided in torsades de pointes. It is an option for hemodynamically stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia instead. Tell: in torsades, the only usable antiarrhythmic is lidocaine.

Beta blockers such as metoprolol are avoided in torsades de pointes because the bradycardia they cause lengthens the R-to-R interval and indirectly prolongs the QT. Tell: her QT is already long, so slowing the heart is harmful.

set2.q: An 82-year-old woman has an electrocardiogram at a routine visit and has no symptoms. The rhythm is regular at 70, every P wave is followed by a narrow QRS, and the PR interval is a constant 0.26 seconds. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mobitz type II has a constant PR, usually in the normal range, with randomly dropped QRS complexes. Every one of her P waves is followed by a QRS, and her PR of 0.26 seconds is long. Tell: no dropped beats means no second-degree block.
ruled out by a stated finding

Third-degree block shows P waves with no relationship to the QRS complexes and a ventricular rate usually under 40. She conducts every P wave at a rate of 70. Tell: a fixed PR before every QRS rules out complete block.

Correct. A regular rhythm with every P wave followed by a narrow QRS and a constant PR of 0.26 seconds (over 0.20) is first-degree atrioventricular block. The vast majority cause no symptoms, and at 82 the most common cause, age-related degeneration of the conduction system, fits; no treatment is needed.
Mobitz type I lengthens the PR progressively until a QRS drops. Her PR is long but constant at 0.26 seconds, and every P wave conducts. Tell: a constant PR with no drops is first degree.
ruled out by a stated finding

set2.q: A 71-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy and a reduced ejection fraction has worsening dyspnea and fatigue despite medical therapy. His electrocardiogram shows a QRS of 0.16 seconds with a dominant S wave in V1 and monophasic R waves in I, V5 and V6. Which is the most appropriate treatment for this conduction problem?
opts: Most left bundle branch block is left untreated, but he is the exception: symptomatic block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, which gets a biventricular pacemaker. Tell: his worsening dyspnea and fatigue despite therapy move him past observation.

Catheter ablation cannot restore conduction through a blocked left bundle. His wide QRS with a dominant S in V1 and monophasic lateral R waves is left bundle branch block, and with symptoms and a reduced ejection fraction it is treated with a biventricular pacemaker. Tell: block plus low ejection fraction means biventricular pacing.

Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia; left bundle branch block is a conduction delay, not a fast rhythm. With symptoms and a reduced ejection fraction, he needs a biventricular pacemaker. Tell: there is no tachycardia here to convert.

Correct. A QRS of 0.16 seconds with a dominant S wave in V1 and monophasic R waves in I, V5 and V6 is left bundle branch block, and dilated cardiomyopathy is a named cause. The block is usually left untreated, except symptomatic block with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, exactly his case, which gets a biventricular pacemaker.

set2.q: A 22-year-old man has sudden palpitations and lightheadedness. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 112/70. His 12-lead electrocardiogram is shown. Which drug is the most appropriate?
opts: Lidocaine is not the listed drug for this rhythm. The look-alike wide rhythm, ventricular tachycardia, is regular at 150 to 200, whereas this one is irregular with rates approaching 300, which marks atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: irregularity separates the two.

Correct. The tracing shows a very fast, irregular rhythm with wide complexes of changing width, which is atrial fibrillation conducting with Wolff-Parkinson-White (pre-excited atrial fibrillation). He is alert with a blood pressure of 112/70, and in this setting intravenous procainamide is used, never adenosine.

Adenosine must never be used when atrial fibrillation runs with Wolff-Parkinson-White; it is first line only for ordinary orthodromic reentry. His irregular, wide-complex rhythm of changing width is pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Tell: irregular wide complexes in a young man with palpitations rule adenosine out and point to procainamide.

Intravenous rate control is the step for ordinary, stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, which has narrow complexes. His irregular, wide complexes of changing width show conduction down an accessory pathway, which is treated with intravenous procainamide. Tell: wide, irregular and very fast means pre-excited fibrillation, not routine rate control.

set2.q: A 77-year-old woman has no symptoms, but her routine electrocardiogram shows P waves at a steady rate with a constant PR interval and an occasional P wave not followed by a QRS. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Correct. Steady P waves, a constant PR and an occasional P wave without a QRS are Mobitz type II block. It is considered dangerous even without symptoms because of its unpredictable progression to complete block and sudden cardiac death, and its escape rhythm is weak and unreliable; the definitive treatment is a permanent pacemaker.

Observation suits asymptomatic first-degree or Mobitz type I block, not this pattern. A constant PR with an occasional dropped QRS is Mobitz type II, considered dangerous even without symptoms. Tell: in type II, the lack of symptoms does not buy time.

Beta blockers are listed causes of first-degree and Mobitz type I block, not a treatment for block. Mobitz type II, even without symptoms, needs a permanent pacemaker. Tell: rate-slowing drugs belong on the cause list, not the treatment list.

Catheter ablation is itself a listed cause of Mobitz type II block, so it cannot treat it. Her constant PR with an occasional dropped QRS is Mobitz type II, treated definitively with a permanent pacemaker. Tell: a procedure that causes a block cannot fix it.

set2.q: A 79-year-old woman has spells of a racing heartbeat followed by near-fainting. Her ambulatory monitor strip is shown, and her near-fainting spells match the long pauses. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Observation is appropriate in sick sinus syndrome only when symptoms do not correlate with episodes of bradycardia. Her near-fainting spells match the long pauses on her monitor. Tell: correlation between symptoms and pauses moves management from watching to a permanent pacemaker.
ruled out by a stated finding

Atropine is first line for acute, symptomatic, hemodynamically unstable bradycardia, a short-term rescue. Her problem is recurrent, documented pauses from a diseased sinus node, which needs a permanent pacemaker. Tell: acute and unstable means atropine; recurrent and symptomatic means a permanent pacemaker.

Adenosine is used for stable supraventricular tachycardia after a vagal maneuver, to convert the rhythm or slow it. Her near-fainting comes from the pauses, and slowing her heart would not help them. Tell: in tachy-brady syndrome, symptoms that match the pauses call for a permanent pacemaker.

Correct. Bursts of a racing rhythm that stop into long pauses are tachy-brady syndrome, a form of sick sinus syndrome, and her near-fainting matches the pauses. When symptoms correlate with the bradycardia, a permanent pacemaker is the treatment, and tachy-brady syndrome often needs one.
set2.alt: Three rows of a rhythm strip: bursts of rapid narrow complexes that stop abruptly, then long flat pauses before slower beats resume

set2.q: An 81-year-old man reports dizziness and two fainting spells. His pulse is 36, and his rhythm strip is shown, with arrows marking R waves and P waves. Which description best fits this tracing?
opts: PR lengthens until a QRS is dropped

Progressive PR lengthening before a dropped QRS is Mobitz type I. Here the P waves keep no consistent relationship to the QRS complexes at all. Tell: an orderly lengthening pattern is type I; no pattern at all is complete block.
Constant PR with an occasional dropped QRS

A constant PR with an occasional dropped QRS is Mobitz type II. On this strip the distance from each P wave to the next QRS changes every beat, and most P waves are not followed by a QRS. Tell: if no PR repeats, it is not second-degree block.
Every P wave conducted with a long PR

A long, constant PR with every P wave conducted is first-degree block. Here most P waves are not followed by a QRS, and P waves and QRS complexes run at different rates. Tell: far more P waves than QRS complexes rules out first degree.
P waves and QRS complexes at unrelated rates

Correct. The P waves march at their own regular rate and the slow, wide QRS complexes at another, with no fixed relationship: complete dissociation of the atria from the ventricles, third-degree (complete) block, with a ventricular rate usually under 40. His syncope carries an increased risk of sudden death.
set2.alt: Rhythm strip with regularly spaced P waves (upward arrows) and slower complexes (downward arrows) that fall at varying distances from the P waves

set2.q: A 59-year-old woman with crushing chest pain becomes lightheaded but stays awake, with a pulse and a blood pressure of 104/66. Her QT interval was normal on a tracing an hour ago, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Synchronized cardioversion is for unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a pulse. Her strip shows complexes that keep changing shape, so the rhythm is polymorphic and is defibrillated. Tell: a changing QRS shape means an unsynchronized shock.

Intravenous amiodarone may be added after the shock, but drug therapy alone is for stable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia. Polymorphic tachycardia is never truly stable, even in a patient who is awake. Tell: a polymorphic strip means defibrillation first.

Intravenous magnesium breaks torsades de pointes, the polymorphic tachycardia of a prolonged QT. Her QT was normal an hour ago, and polymorphic tachycardia without a long QT is most often from acute ischemia, so she is defibrillated. Tell: magnesium needs a long QT.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Wide complexes that keep changing shape are polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, and with a normal QT and crushing chest pain, acute ischemia is the most common cause. Even though she is awake with a pulse, polymorphic tachycardia is never truly stable, so she is defibrillated, then sent for urgent coronary angiography.

set2.q: An 80-year-old man is brought in dizzy and confused, with a blood pressure of 78/44. His electrocardiogram shows P waves at 76 and wide QRS complexes at 32, with no relationship between them. Which is the most appropriate emergent treatment?
opts: Correct. P waves at 76 and wide QRS complexes at 32 with no relationship are third-degree (complete) block. His confusion and blood pressure of 78/44 call for emergent treatment: atropine or epinephrine, both controversial, or transcutaneous pacing, followed definitively by a permanent pacemaker.

A permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for complete block, but this man is confused with a blood pressure of 78/44, so he needs emergent transcutaneous pacing first. Tell: 'emergent' points to the temporary bridge, not the permanent device.

Synchronized cardioversion shocks an unstable tachycardia; this is a slow escape rhythm at 32 from complete block. An unstable patient with complete block needs transcutaneous pacing. Tell: pace the slow, shock the fast.

Intravenous amiodarone treats ventricular tachycardia, a fast wide rhythm. His wide complexes at 32 are a slow escape rhythm from complete block, which needs transcutaneous pacing. Tell: a slow wide rhythm is an escape rhythm, not tachycardia.
