set2.q: A 74-year-old man with diabetes is told his new palpitations come from atrial fibrillation. Which description best fits his electrocardiogram?
opts: Irregularly irregular, with no P waves

Correct. Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular with absent P waves and no PR interval, and the QRS stays narrow. The rate is often 110 to 160 but can be under 80 or over 200, and diabetes, as in this man, is one of the conditions in which it is commonly seen.
Regular, with sawtooth waves between beats

Regular sawtooth waves between beats describe atrial flutter, in which the atria fire at 250 or more and the node blocks some impulses, most often 2:1. Atrial fibrillation has no organized atrial waves and an irregularly irregular rhythm. Tell: organized sawtooth means flutter; no P waves and no regularity mean fibrillation.
Regular, with a P wave before each beat

A regular rhythm with a uniform P wave before each QRS describes a sinus rhythm, such as sinus tachycardia. Atrial fibrillation has absent P waves and is irregularly irregular. Tell: regularity with a P wave before every beat rules atrial fibrillation out.
Irregular, with three or more P-wave shapes

Irregular beats with three or more P-wave shapes in the same lead describe multifocal atrial tachycardia, from multiple atrial foci, with one P wave per QRS. Atrial fibrillation has no P waves to count. Tell: in an irregular rhythm, changing P shapes mean multifocal; absent P waves mean fibrillation.

set2.q: A 41-year-old woman has had palpitations for a month. The monitor reads a regular rate of 130, and her rhythm strip is shown. Which of the following would most likely account for this rhythm?
opts: Correct. A regular rhythm at 130 with a P wave before every narrow QRS is sinus tachycardia, which is usually the result of a physiologic or pathologic process. Hyperthyroidism is one of the listed pathologic causes, alongside hypovolemia, anemia, hypoxia, pulmonary embolism and myocardial infarction, and it fits a month of palpitations.

Hypothyroidism is a listed cause of sinus bradycardia and of sick sinus syndrome, slowing the sinus rate below 60. Her sinus rhythm is fast at 130. Tell: the thyroid pair splits by direction; hyperthyroidism is on the list of pathologic causes of sinus tachycardia, hypothyroidism on the slow list.

Digoxin is listed with beta blockers and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers as a drug cause of sinus bradycardia; it slows the sinus rate. The drug causes of sinus tachycardia are stimulants, anticholinergics, or abrupt withdrawal of a beta blocker or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Tell: digoxin belongs on the slow list.

Increased intracranial pressure is listed among the causes of sinus bradycardia, so it would slow this rhythm below 60, not raise it to 130. A fast sinus rate instead points to causes such as pain, anxiety, hypovolemia, anemia, hypoxia or hyperthyroidism. Tell: raised intracranial pressure goes with a slow sinus rate.

set2.q: A 33-year-old man has had a regular, narrow-complex tachycardia at 190 for an hour. He is alert, with a blood pressure of 124/80. A properly performed vagal maneuver has not converted it. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A permanent pacemaker treats chronic symptomatic bradycardia, such as sick sinus syndrome with symptomatic slow rates. He has a fast, regular narrow tachycardia that a pacemaker would not end. Tell: pacemakers answer slow rhythms; a stable supraventricular tachycardia after a failed vagal maneuver gets adenosine.

Correct. He is stable, alert with a blood pressure of 124/80, and a properly performed vagal maneuver has failed, so adenosine is next for this supraventricular tachycardia. It may be given twice if needed and may convert the rhythm to normal sinus rhythm or at least slow it so any P waves can be seen.

Synchronized cardioversion is immediate treatment for hemodynamically unstable supraventricular tachycardia, the less common presentation. He is alert with a blood pressure of 124/80, so he is stable and the next step is adenosine. Tell: failure of a vagal maneuver alone does not make him unstable.

Intravenous procainamide is used when Wolff-Parkinson-White is known or adenosine reveals atrial fibrillation with Wolff-Parkinson-White, an irregular, wide rhythm. His rhythm is regular and narrow with no pre-excitation described. Tell: a regular narrow rhythm after a failed vagal maneuver goes to adenosine.

set2.q: A 79-year-old woman is brought in after fainting. Her pulse is 34. Her electrocardiogram shows regular P waves at 80 and regular wide QRS complexes at 34, with no fixed relationship between them. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A junctional rhythm does not explain two separate regular rhythms: her regular P waves at 80 run independently of wide QRS complexes at 34. That dissociation defines third-degree (complete) block. Tell: two independent rates mean third degree.

Sinus bradycardia would have one P wave before every QRS at a fixed PR. Her atria beat at 80 while the ventricles beat at 34 with no relationship, which is complete block. Tell: two different rates rule out sinus bradycardia.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Regular P waves at 80 and regular wide QRS complexes at 34 with no fixed relationship are complete dissociation of the atria from the ventricles: third-degree (complete) block, with a ventricular rate usually under 40. Her syncope matters because it is associated with an increased risk of sudden death.

Mobitz type II conducts most P waves with a constant PR and drops an occasional QRS. Here no P wave has a fixed relationship to any QRS, and the ventricular rate is 34. Tell: if no PR is fixed, it is complete block, not second degree.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with a prior myocardial infarction has a regular, wide-complex tachycardia at 160 on the monitor. He is alert, with no chest pain or shortness of breath and a blood pressure of 128/80. He has intravenous access and oxygen. Which test belongs in his initial management?
opts: Ambulatory monitoring captures intermittent rhythms over time, but his tachycardia is happening now. Initial management of stable sustained ventricular tachycardia includes a 12-lead electrocardiogram, with a cardiac monitor, intravenous access, oxygen and labs. Tell: a rhythm on the monitor now gets a 12-lead now.

A stroke-risk score is not part of the initial management of ventricular tachycardia. Stable sustained ventricular tachycardia calls for a cardiac monitor, intravenous access, a 12-lead electrocardiogram, oxygen and labs. Tell: the listed steps are monitor, access, 12-lead, oxygen and labs.

Correct. He is alert with a normal blood pressure and no chest pain or dyspnea, so his sustained ventricular tachycardia is stable. Initial management for all patients is a cardiac monitor, intravenous access, a 12-lead electrocardiogram, supplemental oxygen and labs; with access and oxygen in place, the 12-lead comes next, before drug cardioversion.

Urgent coronary angiography follows defibrillation of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. A stable, regular wide tachycardia calls first for the standard initial steps, including a 12-lead electrocardiogram and labs. Tell: regular and stable means workup and drugs, not the catheterization lab.
